question_text: When the price of a mobile voice call rises by 10 percent and, as a result, the demand for SMS messages increases by 15 percent, the cross-price elasticity of demand between calls and SMS is positive. This indicates the two services are:
options: Complementary goods — consumers buy more of both when the price of calls rises
Substitute goods — consumers switch from calls to SMS as calls become more expensive
Independent goods — the demand for SMS is unrelated to the price of calls
Inferior goods — the demand for SMS falls as consumer incomes rise
correct_answer: Substitute goods — consumers switch from calls to SMS as calls become more expensive

question_text: When consumer incomes rise by 10 percent and demand for broadband services rises by 18 percent, the income elasticity of demand for broadband is greater than one. This classifies broadband as:
options: A luxury (income-elastic) good, whose demand rises proportionally faster than income
A necessity (income-inelastic) good, whose demand barely changes with income
An inferior good, whose overall demand actually falls whenever income rises
A Giffen good, whose quantity demanded oddly rises as its own price increases
correct_answer: A luxury (income-elastic) good, whose demand rises proportionally faster than income

question_text: In a competitive telecom market, consumer surplus represents:
options: The extra profit that a firm earns by charging a price that is well above its own costs
The difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a service and what they actually pay
The overall reduction in quantity demanded that is caused by a sudden increase in price
The specific share of the tax burden that is borne by consumers after a new excise tax
correct_answer: The difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a service and what they actually pay

question_text: When a monopolist restricts output below the socially efficient level and raises the price, the economic loss to society compared with the competitive outcome is called:
options: Deadweight loss
Consumer surplus
Producer surplus
Tax incidence
correct_answer: Deadweight loss

question_text: A mobile platform operator charges low prices to consumers to attract a large user base, and then charges higher prices to businesses that wish to reach those consumers through advertising or app stores. This business model is characteristic of:
options: A perfectly competitive market in which numerous small firms are price-takers facing an identical market price
A natural monopoly, where one large network serves the whole market at a lower cost than several rivals could
A two-sided (or multi-sided) market, where the platform intermediates two distinct customer groups
A command economy in which a central authority sets the prices faced by each separate group of consumers
correct_answer: A two-sided (or multi-sided) market, where the platform intermediates two distinct customer groups

question_text: A social messaging application becomes more valuable to each new user as more people already use it, because more connections are possible. Economists call this phenomenon:
options: A positive network externality (or network effect)
A negative externality, where each new user imposes costs on existing users
Economies of scale, where average costs fall as output rises
Price discrimination, where different users are charged different prices
correct_answer: A positive network externality (or network effect)

question_text: A mobile subscriber who has accumulated loyalty points, contacts stored in a proprietary format, and a memorable number that cannot be easily ported faces high switching costs. High switching costs benefit the incumbent operator primarily by:
options: Lowering the average operational cost of serving a subscriber, because loyalty schemes are cheap to run
Strengthening the incentive for new firms to enter, since locked-in customers are seen as easy targets
Reducing the competitive pressure it faces, since subscribers find it costly to move to rivals
Shifting a share of its existing subscribers across to competing networks as their contracts gradually lapse
correct_answer: Reducing the competitive pressure it faces, since subscribers find it costly to move to rivals

question_text: A fixed-line operator has laid fibre-optic cable across an entire city. This investment is largely non-recoverable if the operator exits the market. Such costs are termed:
options: Variable costs, which change with the volume of traffic carried
Opportunity costs, which represent the next-best foregone alternative
External costs, which are imposed on parties outside the transaction
Sunk costs
correct_answer: Sunk costs

question_text: A firm whose average cost per subscriber falls steadily as it adds more subscribers is said to exhibit:
options: Diseconomies of scale, where average cost rises as output increases
Economies of scale
Constant returns to scale, where average cost does not change with output
Diminishing marginal utility, where each extra unit provides less satisfaction
correct_answer: Economies of scale

question_text: In a contestable market, even a single firm may price competitively because:
options: The government fixes prices at the competitive level by decree, leaving the firm little discretion over its tariffs
The incumbent restrains its own profit margins as a gesture of corporate social responsibility toward its users
Sunk costs across the industry are so high that a would-be rival could not recover the fixed capital needed to enter
The threat of potential entry by rivals constrains the incumbent from raising prices above competitive levels
correct_answer: The threat of potential entry by rivals constrains the incumbent from raising prices above competitive levels

question_text: A telecommunications firm that charges each customer exactly their maximum willingness to pay, thereby extracting all consumer surplus, is practising:
options: Second-degree price discrimination, where prices vary by volume consumed
Third-degree price discrimination, where prices vary by customer group
First-degree (or perfect) price discrimination
Predatory pricing, where prices are set below cost to drive rivals out
correct_answer: First-degree (or perfect) price discrimination

question_text: A mobile operator offers the same data plan at one price to residential customers and a lower price to students, based on the observation that students are more price-sensitive. This is an example of:
options: Third-degree price discrimination, segmenting customers by group elasticity
First-degree price discrimination, where each buyer pays their unique reservation price
Second-degree price discrimination, where prices depend on quantity purchased
Uniform pricing, because the plan content is identical
correct_answer: Third-degree price discrimination, segmenting customers by group elasticity

question_text: A broadband provider charges subscribers a fixed monthly access fee and then an additional per-gigabyte usage charge on top. This pricing structure is called:
options: A flat rate, where one fixed monthly fee covers usage regardless of the volume consumed
Predatory pricing, where prices are set below cost to drive rivals from the market
Resale pricing, where the provider buys capacity wholesale and marks it up for retail
A two-part tariff
correct_answer: A two-part tariff

question_text: The Lerner index measures market power as (Price minus Marginal Cost) divided by Price. A Lerner index of zero indicates:
options: No market power — the firm is pricing at marginal cost, consistent with perfect competition
Substantial market power — the firm is pricing well above its marginal cost of supply
A natural monopoly — a single efficient firm supplies the whole market at least cost
Government-mandated pricing — the regulator sets the firm's prices directly by decree
correct_answer: No market power — the firm is pricing at marginal cost, consistent with perfect competition

question_text: Allocative efficiency in a market is achieved when:
options: A single dominant firm becomes large enough to minimise its own average cost of production across the market
Producers throughout the industry adopt the most technically advanced equipment currently available to them
The government sets and controls the retail price of each separate product traded across the whole economy
Goods and services are produced in the quantities that consumers value them, at prices that reflect true costs
correct_answer: Goods and services are produced in the quantities that consumers value them, at prices that reflect true costs

question_text: An operator is productively efficient when it:
options: Sets its retail prices exactly equal to those charged by its nearest competitor
Allocates its output strictly in proportion to the annual incomes of its individual customers
Earns a rate of return that is exactly equal to the prevailing market rate of interest
Produces its output at the lowest possible cost, given current technology and input prices
correct_answer: Produces its output at the lowest possible cost, given current technology and input prices

question_text: A regulatory policy that sacrifices short-term competition concerns in order to encourage investment in next-generation infrastructure is prioritising:
options: Dynamic efficiency — the ability of the market to innovate and improve over time
Allocative efficiency — matching quantities produced to consumer preferences
Productive efficiency — minimising the cost of current output
Regulatory capture — the regulator acting in the interest of the regulated firm
correct_answer: Dynamic efficiency — the ability of the market to innovate and improve over time

question_text: A mobile market with three operators, each aware that its pricing decisions will provoke a response from the other two, is best described as an:
options: Perfect competition, where no single firm influences price
Oligopoly
Natural monopoly, where a single firm serves the whole market at least cost
Monopsony, where a single buyer faces many sellers
correct_answer: Oligopoly

question_text: An incumbent operator temporarily prices a service below its cost of provision with the intention of forcing a new entrant out of the market, after which it plans to raise prices. This behaviour is known as:
options: Penetration pricing, aimed at legitimately building market share
Marginal cost pricing, required of regulated dominant firms
Predatory pricing
Price discrimination, charging different buyers different prices
correct_answer: Predatory pricing

question_text: A telecom operator sells broadband, mobile and television services together at a combined price lower than the sum of their individual prices, requiring customers to subscribe to all three. This commercial strategy is called:
options: Disaggregated resale, where services are sold separately at wholesale
Co-location, where competitors share the operator's physical infrastructure
Resale, where an operator buys wholesale services and retails them
Bundling
correct_answer: Bundling

question_text: Regulators use the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) to measure market concentration. An HHI approaching 10,000 indicates:
options: A perfectly competitive market populated by many small equal-sized firms
A market in which the two largest firms each hold roughly half of the shares
A highly concentrated market approaching a single-firm monopoly
A market so fragmented that it falls below the threshold for regulatory oversight
correct_answer: A highly concentrated market approaching a single-firm monopoly

question_text: In mobile markets, spectrum licences granted to a limited number of operators create a barrier to entry because:
options: Holding a spectrum licence confers a legal monopoly on the licensee for the duration of its term
A firm may use spectrum without a licence once it registers its equipment directly with the ITU
Spectrum is treated as an abundant resource whose use rarely calls for active regulatory management
A new firm cannot launch a mobile network without spectrum, which is scarce and tightly regulated
correct_answer: A new firm cannot launch a mobile network without spectrum, which is scarce and tightly regulated

question_text: Under rate-of-return regulation the regulator sets the allowed profit level, while under price-cap regulation it sets a ceiling on prices. A main advantage of price-cap regulation over rate-of-return is that it:
options: Gives the firm an incentive to cut costs, since it keeps any efficiency gains as extra profit
Assures the regulated firm of a return that at least matches its own cost of capital each year
Removes the regulator's need to gather detailed financial data on the firm's underlying costs
Holds retail prices fixed from year to year, thereby offering consumers a degree of certainty
correct_answer: Gives the firm an incentive to cut costs, since it keeps any efficiency gains as extra profit

question_text: A mobile operator that also owns the towers its competitors must use is said to be vertically integrated. A regulatory concern with vertical integration is that the firm may:
options: Be unable to price its own retail services competitively unless it receives an ongoing government subsidy to do so
Favour its own downstream retail operations by providing rivals with degraded or overpriced access to the towers
Reduce the quality of its own retail services, because managing both network and retail stretches it too thinly
Lose much of its market power at the point of integration, as combining the two layers invites closer scrutiny
correct_answer: Favour its own downstream retail operations by providing rivals with degraded or overpriced access to the towers

question_text: Economic theory defines a public good as one that is non-rival and non-excludable. A broadcast radio signal most closely resembles:
options: A public good
A private good, because the broadcaster can charge for each listener
A club good, because it is non-rival but perfectly excludable
A common resource, because use by one person diminishes supply for others
correct_answer: A public good

question_text: Structural separation in a telecom market means:
options: The telecom regulator itself divides its own internal functions across several distinct and separately managed government departments
Competing operators in the market are required to share their customer databases with one another on demand
The monopoly infrastructure (such as the local loop) is owned by a separate company from the retail service providers that use it
The government privatises the incumbent operator by selling its shares directly to members of the general public
correct_answer: The monopoly infrastructure (such as the local loop) is owned by a separate company from the retail service providers that use it

question_text: Accounting separation requires a vertically integrated operator to:
options: Physically and legally split its wholesale and retail operations into two distinct companies, each placed under its own independent management
Keep separate financial accounts for its wholesale network and its retail service divisions, as though they were independent entities
Share the whole of its detailed internal financial accounts freely with each of its rival operators in the market
File one identical set of financial statements across each of the separate countries in which it happens to operate
correct_answer: Keep separate financial accounts for its wholesale network and its retail service divisions, as though they were independent entities

question_text: A universal service obligation (USO) in telecommunications is best defined as:
options: A requirement that each licensed operator provide all the services it currently offers free of charge to the households it serves
An international treaty that bars a signatory country from placing restrictions on its own domestic telecommunications market at will
A regulatory requirement that certain basic services are made available to all citizens at an affordable price, regardless of location
A licence condition that bars a dominant firm from raising the retail prices of its regulated basic services once these are set
correct_answer: A regulatory requirement that certain basic services are made available to all citizens at an affordable price, regardless of location

question_text: When the provision of universal service is commercially unviable in high-cost rural areas, regulators commonly establish:
options: A regulated price floor that prevents operators from discounting their services in profitable urban areas
A mandatory transfer of spectrum rights from profitable operators to unprofitable rural operators
A direct legal obligation requiring consumers themselves to subsidise rural service providers
A universal service fund financed by levies on operators in proportion to their revenues
correct_answer: A universal service fund financed by levies on operators in proportion to their revenues

question_text: Market failure due to information asymmetry occurs when:
options: Both buyers and sellers happen to hold much the same information about the product's underlying quality
One side of a market has substantially more information than the other, preventing efficient transactions
The government itself holds more information than the market does about the quantities that should be produced
A single firm sustains lower costs than its rivals over time because of the proprietary technology it owns
correct_answer: One side of a market has substantially more information than the other, preventing efficient transactions

question_text: A positive externality exists when:
options: A transaction between a buyer and seller generates benefits for third parties who are not part of the transaction
A firm knowingly imposes ongoing costs on the wider society that it does not itself have to bear or pay for
A government tax deliberately corrects an existing, persistent over-supply of some particular harmful good
A monopoly firm simply charges its customers a retail price that sits above the competitive market price
correct_answer: A transaction between a buyer and seller generates benefits for third parties who are not part of the transaction

question_text: Ex-ante regulation differs from ex-post regulation in that ex-ante:
options: Intervention by the regulator takes place after a breach has already been detected and formally proven to have occurred
Regulators choose to lean on general competition law in place of dedicated sector-specific rules and remedies
Firms remain free to set their own commercial terms right up until a formal complaint is eventually received
Rules are set in advance to shape market behaviour before problems arise, rather than reacting to them after the fact
correct_answer: Rules are set in advance to shape market behaviour before problems arise, rather than reacting to them after the fact

question_text: An operator designated as having Significant Market Power (SMP) is one that:
options: Simply holds an operating licence that happens to run for a fixed term of fewer than five years in total duration
Enjoys a position of economic strength that allows it to behave to an appreciable extent independently of competitors, customers and consumers
Reports annual revenues that consistently fall below the national regulatory authority's own official reporting threshold for the sector
Operates within remote rural districts where it faces little urban competition and serves a small, dispersed subscriber base
correct_answer: Enjoys a position of economic strength that allows it to behave to an appreciable extent independently of competitors, customers and consumers

question_text: Before assessing whether an operator has SMP, a regulator must first define the relevant market. The relevant product market is defined as:
options: The complete range of products offered by each licensed operator across the whole of the country
Whatever products the regulator personally decides to regulate in pursuit of its own policy aims
The smallest set of products that are close enough substitutes to constrain each other's prices
Just the services that happen to be covered by the dominant operator's own individual licence
correct_answer: The smallest set of products that are close enough substitutes to constrain each other's prices

question_text: A 'bottleneck' facility in telecommunications is one that:
options: Sits at the exact geographic centre of the national telecommunications network, midway between its main exchanges
May be used by the incumbent operator under the specific terms that are written into the incumbent's own licence
Is shared on a voluntary basis by the operators in the market under the terms of a formal co-regulation agreement
Is essential for reaching end customers, and which competitors cannot duplicate economically, giving the owner market power
correct_answer: Is essential for reaching end customers, and which competitors cannot duplicate economically, giving the owner market power

question_text: Local loop unbundling (LLU) allows:
options: Alternative operators to rent the physical copper or fibre pair between the exchange and a customer's premises from the incumbent, at regulated prices
The incumbent operator to make use of rival operators' own transmission equipment without paying them a charge for it
Individual consumers to take permanent personal ownership of the physical cable that runs between their premises and the exchange
Operators to resell one another's retail services to customers without holding a network of their own, buying capacity wholesale instead
correct_answer: Alternative operators to rent the physical copper or fibre pair between the exchange and a customer's premises from the incumbent, at regulated prices

question_text: Tariff rebalancing in the telecom sector typically refers to:
options: Raising each category of retail price by the same uniform percentage across the board, simply to reflect the annual rate of price inflation
Shifting the burden of spectrum licence charges away from the mobile operators so that the fixed-line operators come to bear these costs instead
Adjusting prices so that each service covers its cost, reducing cross-subsidies — for instance, raising local call prices and lowering international prices
Setting one uniform schedule of retail prices for the operators regardless of each firm's own underlying cost structure or overall size
correct_answer: Adjusting prices so that each service covers its cost, reducing cross-subsidies — for instance, raising local call prices and lowering international prices

question_text: An operator is likely to retain structural dominance even after market liberalisation largely because it:
options: Has already lost the great majority of its existing subscribers over to the rival firms that recently entered the market
Controls legacy infrastructure (such as the local loop or backhaul) that new entrants cannot easily or economically replicate
Holds an operating licence that happened to be issued in the period just after the wider market was first opened up
Provides very few retail services of its own in the newly opened and now fully competitive downstream retail market
correct_answer: Controls legacy infrastructure (such as the local loop or backhaul) that new entrants cannot easily or economically replicate

question_text: A regulatory impact assessment (RIA) is designed to:
options: Audit the detailed financial accounts of a regulated company in the aftermath of a breach it has already committed
Determine the precise size of the financial penalty to impose on an operator that has been found guilty of market abuse
Estimate the costs and benefits of a proposed regulatory intervention before it is implemented, to ensure its net effect is positive
Formally replace the entire public consultation process with a single short internal report drafted by the regulator's staff
correct_answer: Estimate the costs and benefits of a proposed regulatory intervention before it is implemented, to ensure its net effect is positive

question_text: A light-touch regulatory approach is typically characterised by:
options: Minimal intervention, with the regulator stepping in only when there is clear market failure or a specific complaint
Detailed, highly prescriptive rules that govern each separate aspect of an operator's day-to-day behaviour
The outright nationalisation of the dominant operator, undertaken chiefly to head off future price abuses
Prohibiting rival forms of competition outright in order to protect the position of the existing natural monopoly
correct_answer: Minimal intervention, with the regulator stepping in only when there is clear market failure or a specific complaint

question_text: Functional separation requires a dominant operator to:
options: Sell off its entire network infrastructure outright to a genuinely independent and unrelated third-party company at its full market value
Provide the same wholesale prices to retail rivals as it charges its own retail division, well ahead of the point at which formal separation occurs
Establish a distinct universal service fund that is financed out of its own revenues, drawing on no outside contributions or support from others
Operate its wholesale access network as a functionally separate business unit with independent management and systems, even if ownership remains unified
correct_answer: Operate its wholesale access network as a functionally separate business unit with independent management and systems, even if ownership remains unified

question_text: The main argument in favour of infrastructure competition (multiple physical networks) over service competition (multiple retailers on one network) is that it:
options: Leads to greater dynamic efficiency and innovation as firms compete across multiple layers of the value chain
Reduces the total overall cost of building out broadband networks right across the whole of the country
Is readily achievable even in rural areas, where the economics may support just a single viable network
Removes the need for access regulation once the competing physical networks have been fully built out
correct_answer: Leads to greater dynamic efficiency and innovation as firms compete across multiple layers of the value chain

question_text: Regulators have intervened in international roaming markets because:
options: Roaming agreements freely negotiated between operators are explicitly prohibited under the WTO Basic Telecommunications Agreement
Roaming charges were often far above cost, exploiting consumers who had no practical ability to switch provider while abroad
The ITU formally and strictly requires that international calls be routed through a single central global switching hub
Overall consumer demand for roaming services was historically too low to justify commercial provision by operators
correct_answer: Roaming charges were often far above cost, exploiting consumers who had no practical ability to switch provider while abroad

question_text: When a regulator performs a cost-benefit analysis of a proposed remedy, it should compare:
options: The regulator's own annual administrative budget against the total yearly revenue earned by the dominant operator in the market
The average income of subscribers in rural districts against the average income of subscribers living in urban districts
The current market share held by each individual operator against the calculated overall national market average
The direct costs imposed on industry and consumers against the economic benefits of correcting the market failure
correct_answer: The direct costs imposed on industry and consumers against the economic benefits of correcting the market failure

question_text: A multi-sector regulator that oversees telecoms, energy and water simultaneously may have the advantage of:
options: Focusing its specialist expertise narrowly on the single industry with its own particular technical characteristics
Having a considerably larger administrative staff on hand to investigate each individual complaint that is received
Operating at arm's length from government in a way that separate, sector-specific bodies would find hard to match
Applying consistent regulatory principles across sectors and avoiding conflicts between sector-specific agencies
correct_answer: Applying consistent regulatory principles across sectors and avoiding conflicts between sector-specific agencies

question_text: When two large mobile operators propose to merge, reducing the number of national operators from four to three, the regulator's primary competition concern is likely to be:
options: An immediate and unavoidable increase in the spectrum licence costs faced by the newly merged entity
A risk that the newly merged entity will prove unable to recover the licence costs it has taken on
A reduction in competitive pressure that could lead to higher prices or lower investment
A formal requirement that the smaller of the two merged operators buy out the regulator itself
correct_answer: A reduction in competitive pressure that could lead to higher prices or lower investment

question_text: The main advantage of sector-specific telecom regulation over reliance on general competition law is that:
options: Sector-specific rules can be calibrated to the industry's technical characteristics and applied proactively, without waiting for a market abuse to occur
Competition law tends to reach much the same practical outcome as dedicated sector-specific regulation would in a typical case
Sector regulation is inherently more flexible than the alternative, simply because it has no set of prescribed rules for firms to follow
Competition authorities are formally and, in practice, indefinitely forbidden from intervening in the telecom markets under the stated conditions
correct_answer: Sector-specific rules can be calibrated to the industry's technical characteristics and applied proactively, without waiting for a market abuse to occur

question_text: Asymmetric regulation imposes obligations on the dominant operator that are not applied to smaller rivals. The justification for this asymmetry is that:
options: Smaller operators are, on the whole, simply managed better and so they need considerably fewer regulatory rules imposed on them
Only the dominant operator has the market power to harm competition or consumers in ways that the market itself cannot correct
Each operator active in the market ought to be regulated in precisely the same way regardless of the market share it happens to hold
Asymmetric regulation of this specific kind is mandated by the WTO Reference Paper in the great majority of documented cases
correct_answer: Only the dominant operator has the market power to harm competition or consumers in ways that the market itself cannot correct

question_text: Periodic market reviews, in which the regulator reassesses which operators have SMP and what remedies apply, serve primarily to:
options: Steadily ratchet up the regulatory obligations that are placed on operators across the whole market as the years go by
Allow the regulator to raise additional annual licence fees specifically from the dominant operators alone
Ensure that regulatory obligations remain proportionate as market conditions evolve, and are removed when no longer needed
Transfer ownership of the incumbent operator back to the state should effective competition fail to develop
correct_answer: Ensure that regulatory obligations remain proportionate as market conditions evolve, and are removed when no longer needed

question_text: Regulatory forbearance occurs when a regulator:
options: Simply fails to apply its own regulations properly owing to administrative error or chronic under-resourcing
Is formally prevented from intervening in the market by a court injunction that the operator itself had obtained
Deliberately increases the overall stringency of its regulation in response to changing market conditions
Deliberately refrains from exercising its available powers in a market, on the grounds that competition is sufficient
correct_answer: Deliberately refrains from exercising its available powers in a market, on the grounds that competition is sufficient

question_text: Regulatory independence from the regulated industry encompasses institutional, financial and operational dimensions. Which dimension is concerned with ensuring regulators are not housed within the same organisation as operators?
options: Financial independence
Institutional independence
Operational independence
Political independence
correct_answer: Institutional independence

question_text: A key risk where the regulator's annual budget is set entirely at the government's discretion is that:
options: The regulator will often over-spend heavily on enforcement against politically connected firms
Operators will demand the right to audit the regulator's own accounts directly and regularly
The regulator may be starved of resources as an indirect way of constraining its activity
The regulator will, in effect, come to depend on the operators it oversees for its financial survival
correct_answer: The regulator may be starved of resources as an indirect way of constraining its activity

question_text: Which of the following is a mechanism that makes a regulator accountable without compromising its independence?
options: A requirement to publish an annual report explaining its decisions to the legislature and public
Allowing the responsible minister to personally overturn a regulatory decision once it has been made
Requiring the regulated operator itself to formally sign off on regulatory decisions before they take effect
Permitting the regulator to operate freely without publishing the criteria on which its decisions rest
correct_answer: A requirement to publish an annual report explaining its decisions to the legislature and public

question_text: Transparency in regulation requires that:
options: The entire body of correspondence between the regulator and the operators it regulates is to be kept strictly confidential throughout
The regulator shares just its bare final decisions with the public, without publishing the underlying reasoning that led up to them
The criteria, process and reasoning behind regulatory decisions are publicly available so that affected parties can understand and challenge them
Consultation documents produced by the regulator are circulated to the single dominant operator in the market and to no one else
correct_answer: The criteria, process and reasoning behind regulatory decisions are publicly available so that affected parties can understand and challenge them

question_text: Regulatory certainty is valued by investors primarily because:
options: Stable rules tend, over time, to translate into steadily lower retail prices for the great majority of consumers
Predictable rules reduce the risk premium they require when committing long-term capital to network infrastructure
Regulatory certainty of this kind holds back operators that might otherwise enter or exit the market at will
Predictable rules do away with much of the need for a formal licensing process to exist in the first place
correct_answer: Predictable rules reduce the risk premium they require when committing long-term capital to network infrastructure

question_text: Under RPI-X price-cap regulation, if RPI is the retail price index and X is an efficiency factor, operators are required to:
options: Increase their regulated prices by the full RPI each year regardless of their own internal cost savings
Hold their regulated prices fixed in nominal terms year after year, regardless of the ongoing rate of inflation
Reduce their regulated prices in real terms by X per cent per year, passing efficiency gains to consumers
Set their prices at exactly the rate of inflation minus whatever government subsidy happens to apply
correct_answer: Reduce their regulated prices in real terms by X per cent per year, passing efficiency gains to consumers

question_text: A high X factor in a price-cap formula (RPI-X) implies:
options: The regulator expects the operator to achieve large efficiency savings and requires it to pass them on to consumers quickly
The regulator simply expects the wider market to grow steadily less competitive over the course of the coming years
The regulated operator will instead receive a direct annual subsidy equal to X per cent of its total yearly revenues
The entire price cap will be lifted altogether once a fixed period of exactly X years of regulation has finally passed
correct_answer: The regulator expects the operator to achieve large efficiency savings and requires it to pass them on to consumers quickly

question_text: A well-known drawback of rate-of-return (RoR) regulation is that it may create an incentive for the regulated firm to:
options: Under-invest in new infrastructure, holding back on capital projects so as to avoid attracting regulatory scrutiny
Reduce its retail prices below cost, specifically in order to deliberately drive its rivals out of the market
Resist the kinds of technological change that would oblige it to undertake fresh rounds of new capital spending
Over-invest in capital (the Averch-Johnson effect), because profit is calculated as a percentage of the asset base
correct_answer: Over-invest in capital (the Averch-Johnson effect), because profit is calculated as a percentage of the asset base

question_text: A licence condition requiring a mobile operator to achieve a minimum 95 percent population coverage and a maximum 2-second call-setup delay is an example of:
options: Quality-of-service (QoS) regulation imposing minimum performance standards
Price-cap regulation limiting how much the operator may charge
Accounting separation requiring separate financial records
Structural separation requiring distinct ownership of the access network
correct_answer: Quality-of-service (QoS) regulation imposing minimum performance standards

question_text: A regulator that requires a dominant operator to submit annual regulatory accounts broken down by network element cost, retail revenue and margin is using:
options: Accounting separation to improve cost transparency and detect potential cross-subsidies
Structural separation to legally mandate the creation of two separate and distinct companies
A formal price-cap review carried out specifically to determine the operator's new X factor
A formal market review carried out specifically to define the relevant product market
correct_answer: Accounting separation to improve cost transparency and detect potential cross-subsidies

question_text: A regulatory sandbox allows:
options: Operators to remove themselves from most forms of regulation on a voluntary basis for a fixed, set period of time
Governments to informally trial new regulatory agencies in advance of the point at which they are established in law
Firms to test innovative products or business models in a controlled environment with relaxed rules, subject to safeguards
Regulators to impose considerably higher fines on firms than the underlying legislation would normally permit them to
correct_answer: Firms to test innovative products or business models in a controlled environment with relaxed rules, subject to safeguards

question_text: A sunset clause in a regulatory instrument provides that:
options: The regulated firm concerned must fully upgrade its network before a specified statutory deadline arrives
The sitting regulator personally must resign from office once its own five-year term formally ends
The obligations under the licence are instead phased in gradually over the course of several years
The regulation automatically expires after a set time unless the regulator actively decides to renew it
correct_answer: The regulation automatically expires after a set time unless the regulator actively decides to renew it

question_text: During a periodic market review, if the regulator finds that effective competition has developed and the dominant operator no longer has SMP, the appropriate response is to:
options: Remove or relax the sector-specific obligations previously imposed on that operator
Impose considerably stricter conditions specifically to safeguard the competition that has newly emerged
Transfer the operator's own spectrum holdings directly to a separate, state-owned entity instead
Launch a full formal inquiry to determine whether outright re-nationalisation of the firm is needed
correct_answer: Remove or relax the sector-specific obligations previously imposed on that operator

question_text: When an interconnection agreement cannot be reached through commercial negotiation, most regulatory frameworks allow either party to:
options: Withdraw wholesale services from the rival operator until an agreement is finally reached
Refer the dispute to the regulator for binding arbitration or determination
Seek damages directly from the rival operator's own shareholders in a consumer court
Delay interconnection indefinitely, without facing a penalty for the resulting hold-up
correct_answer: Refer the dispute to the regulator for binding arbitration or determination

question_text: Regulatory risk, from the perspective of an investor in telecoms infrastructure, refers to:
options: The physical risk that the operator's network equipment might be seriously damaged by extreme weather events
The risk that the regulator will change the rules in ways that reduce the expected return on invested capital
The risk that existing subscribers will switch across to rival operators once newer services are launched
The risk that competition law will end up prohibiting the operator from charging its cost-based prices
correct_answer: The risk that the regulator will change the rules in ways that reduce the expected return on invested capital

question_text: Monitoring and enforcement are distinct regulatory activities. Monitoring is primarily concerned with:
options: Imposing fines and other penalties on firms that have already formally breached their own licences
Deciding in the first place what specific obligations should be imposed on operators generally
Publishing detailed annual reports covering the regulator's own internal financial performance
Collecting data and tracking compliance with regulatory obligations before a breach has occurred
correct_answer: Collecting data and tracking compliance with regulatory obligations before a breach has occurred

question_text: A regulator that responds to a minor licence breach with an informal warning, escalating to a formal compliance notice and then a fine if the breach persists, is applying:
options: A graduated (or proportionate) enforcement approach
Regulatory capture, whereby the regulator avoids penalising the industry
Co-regulation, where the industry jointly decides on the appropriate penalty
Zero regulation, since no immediate fine is imposed on the first breach
correct_answer: A graduated (or proportionate) enforcement approach

question_text: A voluntary code of practice adopted by operators without legislative force serves primarily to:
options: Replace the formal licence conditions in their entirety with a set of non-binding voluntary commitments made in their place
Establish baseline standards of consumer treatment that operators commit to publicly, creating reputational incentives for compliance
Allow the regulator to impose fines for a breach without first having to work through the usual steps of due process
Transfer the whole of the regulatory responsibility for the matter across to the ordinary courts of law in its place
correct_answer: Establish baseline standards of consumer treatment that operators commit to publicly, creating reputational incentives for compliance

question_text: When a regulator proposes a new interconnection pricing methodology, best practice requires it to publish a consultation document and allow a period for:
options: The responsible government minister to formally approve the document before it is sent out to the operators
The single dominant operator alone to veto proposals that it personally finds commercially disadvantageous
Operators, consumers and other interested parties to comment before the methodology is finalised
The courts to formally pre-approve the methodology as being legally valid before its scheduled publication date
correct_answer: Operators, consumers and other interested parties to comment before the methodology is finalised

question_text: In developing economies, one frequently cited obstacle to effective regulation is:
options: An overall excess of regulatory staff, whose collective activity imposes unnecessary administrative burdens on each licensed operator in the sector
The knowledge and information gap between the regulator and the companies it regulates, due to limited technical and financial expertise in the regulatory body
The outright refusal of the incumbent operators to obey the governing law, whatever the particular circumstances they happen to face
The complete and total absence of legislation of the kind needed to enable the creation of a regulatory body in the very first place
correct_answer: The knowledge and information gap between the regulator and the companies it regulates, due to limited technical and financial expertise in the regulatory body

question_text: Why are licence conditions a particularly powerful regulatory instrument compared with general guidelines?
options: Because informal guidelines tend to be published in the wake of a court order, whereas formal licences issue much faster
Because binding licence conditions apply, without exception, to each firm operating across the sectors of the economy
Because non-binding guidelines must first be approved by the ITU, whereas formal licences need no such prior approval
Because they are legally binding on the licence holder and breach can result in enforcement action or licence revocation
correct_answer: Because they are legally binding on the licence holder and breach can result in enforcement action or licence revocation

question_text: A regulatory requirement for operators to maintain a formal written complaint procedure and respond within a set number of days is designed to:
options: Prevent ordinary consumers from taking their complaints directly to a court or an independent tribunal
Ensure consumers have an accessible redress mechanism and operators take service quality seriously
Transfer consumer protection responsibilities away from the regulator and over to the operator in its place
Allow the operator to legitimately charge consumers a fee for the internal processing of their complaints
correct_answer: Ensure consumers have an accessible redress mechanism and operators take service quality seriously

question_text: Regulators in smaller markets often benchmark their rules and tariff levels against those in comparable countries. The primary purpose of such benchmarking is to:
options: Simply copy the exact rules used by the single largest economy, taking little account of local market conditions back at home
Do away with the whole of the national public consultation process and put an international one in its place altogether
Draw on evidence from multiple markets to set well-informed, defensible regulatory parameters in the absence of sufficient domestic data
Allow individual operators themselves to freely choose whichever country's regulatory framework they would personally prefer
correct_answer: Draw on evidence from multiple markets to set well-informed, defensible regulatory parameters in the absence of sufficient domestic data

question_text: In most countries, the telecommunications regulatory framework assigns the legislature (parliament) the role of:
options: Setting the wholesale interconnection prices individually, on a strict case-by-case basis, each time they arise
Enacting the primary legislation that establishes the regulatory body and confers its powers
Issuing individual operator licences directly and personally handling the spectrum allocation decisions itself
Investigating each individual consumer complaint that is raised about the operators' billing practices
correct_answer: Enacting the primary legislation that establishes the regulatory body and confers its powers

question_text: An independent regulatory authority is often governed by a multi-member board rather than a single regulator. The main benefit of a board structure is that:
options: A multi-member board can issue licences considerably faster because each member simply signs separately
Individual board members are personally and legally liable for regulatory decisions, which deters bias
A multi-member board structure needs no underlying legislation of its own in order to be established
Decisions represent a range of views and are less vulnerable to the bias or capture of any single individual
correct_answer: Decisions represent a range of views and are less vulnerable to the bias or capture of any single individual

question_text: Spectrum refarming refers to the process of:
options: Reassigning spectrum bands previously used by one technology (e.g. 2G) to a newer, more spectrally efficient technology (e.g. 4G or 5G)
Allocating brand-new spectrum bands that were identified for the first time through recent satellite observation work
Transferring spectrum rights on a lasting basis between two or more separate countries under a formal, signed ITU agreement
Increasing the total quantity of MHz available within a given band, simply by cutting down the size of its guard bands further
correct_answer: Reassigning spectrum bands previously used by one technology (e.g. 2G) to a newer, more spectrally efficient technology (e.g. 4G or 5G)

question_text: In spectrum secondary trading, spectrum rights are:
options: Handed straight back to the government for cost-free reallocation once the licensee no longer has a use for them
Auctioned directly by the ITU itself to the single highest bidder drawn from across its various member states
Transferred or leased from one licence holder to another through market transactions, subject to regulator approval
Assigned by default to whichever operator happens to hold the longest network operating history on record
correct_answer: Transferred or leased from one licence holder to another through market transactions, subject to regulator approval

question_text: Cognitive radio technology enables more efficient spectrum use primarily by:
options: Physically expanding the total radio spectrum available worldwide by opening up brand-new, previously untapped frequency ranges for general use
Allowing devices to sense and opportunistically use spectrum bands that are temporarily idle, without causing harmful interference to primary users
Requiring the operators in the market to share a single licensed frequency band between themselves on a lasting, ongoing basis
Replacing the existing licensed spectrum bands with unlicensed, licence-exempt bands right across the range of telecom services
correct_answer: Allowing devices to sense and opportunistically use spectrum bands that are temporarily idle, without causing harmful interference to primary users

question_text: A regulator may impose spectrum caps (or spectrum limits) on individual operators in order to:
options: Ensure that each operator active in the market ends up holding roughly the same overall amount of licensed spectrum
Reduce the total quantity of spectrum that is put to use by the operators taken together across the country
Let the incumbent operator retain the bulk of the remaining spectrum once market liberalisation has occurred
Prevent any single operator from acquiring so much spectrum that it can disadvantage rivals, particularly in auctions
correct_answer: Prevent any single operator from acquiring so much spectrum that it can disadvantage rivals, particularly in auctions

question_text: When a country's radio transmissions could cause interference to services in a neighbouring country, the coordination process is managed through:
options: Bilateral and multilateral agreements, guided by the ITU Radio Regulations
The World Trade Organization's Basic Telecommunications Agreement, negotiated between member states
A dedicated telecommunications sub-committee that operates under the UN Security Council itself
The National Regulatory Authority of the affected country acting on its own initiative, in a unilateral fashion
correct_answer: Bilateral and multilateral agreements, guided by the ITU Radio Regulations

question_text: In the E.164 international numbering plan, a full international telephone number comprises:
options: A network code followed directly by a subscriber number, with an overall minimum of ten digits
A two-letter country prefix followed by both an area code and a separate subscriber number
A country code followed by the national (significant) number, with the total not exceeding 15 digits
A six-digit operator code followed directly by the individual subscriber's own national number
correct_answer: A country code followed by the national (significant) number, with the total not exceeding 15 digits

question_text: Non-geographic numbers differ from geographic numbers in that they:
options: Are not tied to a specific physical location, and are used for services such as freephone, premium-rate, or shared-cost calls
May be assigned to mobile subscribers specifically, and are withheld from customers of the fixed-line operators
Must begin with the full international country code of whichever network happens to originate the particular call in question
Are set aside for the sole use of the emergency services, following a common arrangement adopted across countries
correct_answer: Are not tied to a specific physical location, and are used for services such as freephone, premium-rate, or shared-cost calls

question_text: A freephone (toll-free) service number is one where:
options: Neither the caller nor the called party pays a penny, since the government fully subsidises the cost of the call
The caller instead pays a considerably higher-than-standard rate, which the operator itself then retains
The number in question is available just to emergency services and hospitals, and to nobody besides them
The cost of the call is borne by the called party (the business) rather than the calling consumer
correct_answer: The cost of the call is borne by the called party (the business) rather than the calling consumer

question_text: Premium-rate service numbers expose consumers to the risk of high unintended charges. A common regulatory response is to:
options: Prohibit the use of premium-rate numbers outright, right across the whole of the retail market
Require clear price disclosure before the consumer connects and impose a maximum per-minute or per-call cap
Require that premium-rate calls be paid for in full and in advance by the calling consumer
Let operators set their own premium rates freely, with no obligation to disclose them to callers
correct_answer: Require clear price disclosure before the consumer connects and impose a maximum per-minute or per-call cap

question_text: Short codes (e.g. 3- to 6-digit numbers) are administered by national regulators because:
options: Short codes are instead allocated by the ITU directly to each individual country as one part of the wider E.164 numbering plan
They are a scarce resource — their brevity limits how many exist — and must be allocated fairly across competing service providers
Short codes are effectively abundant in overall supply, and for that reason they call for little in the way of formal administration
Short codes are reserved for use by government agencies and by the telecom regulators themselves, rather than by service providers
correct_answer: They are a scarce resource — their brevity limits how many exist — and must be allocated fairly across competing service providers

question_text: In a standard telephone call, the originating operator is the one that:
options: Receives the call on behalf of the called subscriber and is the network that actually rings their handset
Issues the specific telephone number at which the called party can ultimately be reached by other callers
Carries the call from the calling subscriber and delivers it to the network of the terminating operator
Determines the final retail price that is actually charged to the called party for receiving the call
correct_answer: Carries the call from the calling subscriber and delivers it to the network of the terminating operator

question_text: Mobile termination rates (MTRs) are regulated in many countries because:
options: Mobile operators, as a general rule, charge their own subscribers far too little money for the incoming calls that they receive
The ITU formally and explicitly mandates that mobile termination rates be set at a level of zero across its member states
Mobile termination rates of this kind are paid directly by the government to operators, rather than between the operators
The terminating operator has a monopoly over access to its own subscribers, allowing it to charge above-cost rates to originating operators
correct_answer: The terminating operator has a monopoly over access to its own subscribers, allowing it to charge above-cost rates to originating operators

question_text: Long-run incremental cost (LRIC) is used as a basis for regulated interconnection prices because:
options: It simply measures the actual historic accounting cost that the operator had already spent at some earlier point in the past
It secures for the regulated operator a fixed, government-mandated profit margin, applied specifically to its interconnection traffic
It is simply the particular costing model that the WTO officially prefers for use across cross-border interconnection arrangements
It reflects the efficient forward-looking cost of providing the specific service, excluding costs unrelated to the traffic being terminated
correct_answer: It reflects the efficient forward-looking cost of providing the specific service, excluding costs unrelated to the traffic being terminated

question_text: Retail-minus pricing sets the wholesale access price at:
options: A wholesale access price set quite deliberately well above the incumbent's own retail price, so as to deter the entry of competitors
The incumbent's retail price minus the retail costs (marketing, billing, etc.) it avoids when selling wholesale, ensuring viable retail competition
Zero, on the basis that wholesale network access to the incumbent's network should be provided free of charge to the operators that seek it
The full and complete cost of building a brand-new, fully competing rival network right from scratch, recalculated on each occasion
correct_answer: The incumbent's retail price minus the retail costs (marketing, billing, etc.) it avoids when selling wholesale, ensuring viable retail competition

question_text: Domestic roaming agreements allow a mobile operator to:
options: Offer its own subscribers calls at no charge whenever they make an international visit to a designated partner country
Make lasting use of a foreign operator's own spectrum inside its national borders, with no fixed limit set on the term
Charge its own subscribers a noticeably lower price whenever they happen to be located within their home region
Provide services to its subscribers in geographic areas it does not cover, by using the network of another domestic operator
correct_answer: Provide services to its subscribers in geographic areas it does not cover, by using the network of another domestic operator

question_text: Regulators impose wholesale roaming caps on visited-network operators. The effect of a wholesale roaming cap is to:
options: Prevent home-network operators from being in a position to sign roaming agreements with other operators, whatever the circumstances
Allow subscribers to make free use of whichever network they personally wish, without needing permission from the operators involved
Limit the price that visited-network operators may charge the home-network operator, which can then pass lower retail prices to travelling subscribers
Set the exact retail price that is charged to consumers by the home operator directly, in a strictly unilateral fashion, without exception
correct_answer: Limit the price that visited-network operators may charge the home-network operator, which can then pass lower retail prices to travelling subscribers

question_text: A Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) differs from a full Mobile Network Operator (MNO) in that an MVNO:
options: Owns its own radio spectrum and base stations outright, but chooses not to maintain a retail customer base of its own
Operates within remote rural districts, in the specific areas where the full MNOs happen to have no network coverage of their own
Is licensed under a general class licence that is free of the various conditions attached to the operating licence of a full MNO
Does not own radio spectrum or a radio access network, and instead buys wholesale network access from an MNO to sell services to end customers
correct_answer: Does not own radio spectrum or a radio access network, and instead buys wholesale network access from an MNO to sell services to end customers

question_text: Passive infrastructure sharing involves operators sharing:
options: Physical structures such as towers, masts, ducts and shelters, without sharing the active radio or transmission equipment
The exact same radio frequencies and active antennas installed together on one single, shared cell site
Spectrum licences themselves, so that both operators end up transmitting together on one single common frequency band
Customer billing systems and subscriber management platforms used internally and separately by each individual operator
correct_answer: Physical structures such as towers, masts, ducts and shelters, without sharing the active radio or transmission equipment

question_text: Radio Access Network (RAN) sharing goes beyond passive sharing in that operators share:
options: The active radio equipment (antennas, transceivers, controllers) in addition to towers and other physical structures
Just the masts and the shelters themselves, but not the associated electronic radio equipment mounted on top of them
Core network elements, such as the central switching and routing infrastructure that is used by each of the operators
Spectrum licences, so that each operator taking part in the shared RAN transmits on one common frequency band
correct_answer: The active radio equipment (antennas, transceivers, controllers) in addition to towers and other physical structures

question_text: Net neutrality is the principle that:
options: Officially designated neutral third parties are the sole entities permitted to operate the internet exchange points
Internet service providers must provide free-of-charge access to the official government websites and to those alone
Internet service providers must treat all internet traffic equally, without discriminating based on source, destination or content type
Content companies must instead pay individual consumers directly for the privilege of consuming their own online services
correct_answer: Internet service providers must treat all internet traffic equally, without discriminating based on source, destination or content type

question_text: In mobile number portability (MNP), the 'losing' operator is:
options: The operator that is actively gaining the subscriber who wishes to keep hold of their existing number
The operator from which the subscriber is porting away — the one that currently holds the number
The operator responsible for routing the ported call once the entire porting process is complete
The operator that centrally administers the national number portability database for the whole industry
correct_answer: The operator from which the subscriber is porting away — the one that currently holds the number

question_text: Regulators that set maximum porting timelines (e.g. one working day) do so primarily to:
options: Prevent operators from using slow porting processes to discourage subscribers from switching
Allow operators to complete the technical work involved before the customer becomes aware of the port
Ensure that porting requests are, as a matter of routine, processed strictly in the order received
Limit the number of porting requests that an operator has to handle over the course of a given month
correct_answer: Prevent operators from using slow porting processes to discourage subscribers from switching

question_text: A short licence duration (e.g. five years) compared with a long one (e.g. twenty years) gives the regulator more:
options: Greater certainty for investors who specifically need predictable returns over a much longer period
A longer interval before a formal regulatory review of the operator's own conduct falls due for hearing
Opportunities to revise the licence conditions as market and technology conditions change
Additional spectrum allocation rights that can then be distributed out to brand-new market entrants
correct_answer: Opportunities to revise the licence conditions as market and technology conditions change

question_text: When renewing a licence, a regulator may attach new or revised conditions. The main constraint on this power is that:
options: No fresh conditions of the kind in question may be added to an existing licence once it has first been granted to the operator
The ITU itself is the sole body permitted to formally approve fresh conditions that come to be added at the point of a licence renewal
New conditions must be proportionate, justified by current market circumstances, and the operator must have fair notice and an opportunity to respond
The national government treasury must separately approve each individual new condition, assessing it for its own fiscal impact first
correct_answer: New conditions must be proportionate, justified by current market circumstances, and the operator must have fair notice and an opportunity to respond

question_text: A regulatory requirement that all licensed operators connect emergency calls free of charge, even when a subscriber has no credit, is justified on the basis that:
options: Emergency calls actually generate significant revenue that fully offsets their own zero-price status
Emergency call access is a fundamental public interest obligation that overrides commercial pricing considerations
The WTO's Basic Telecommunications Agreement explicitly prohibits the levying of a charge for emergency service calls
Subscribers who personally call emergency services are later refunded directly by the government itself
correct_answer: Emergency call access is a fundamental public interest obligation that overrides commercial pricing considerations
